LANSING, Mich. — The National All-Domain Warfighting Center (NADWC), including the Alpena Combat Readiness Training Center (CRTC), will host Silent Swarm 26, July 13–24, with the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Crane Division (NSWC Crane), serving as the lead agency for the advanced uncrewed systems exercise.

The exercise, part of NSWC Crane’s scientific mission, includes experimentation with technologies that can be employed on small multi-domain unmanned systems and may include manned/unmanned surface vessels in the water and small unmanned airborne systems. The results from these experiments will improve spectrum maneuver and resilience capabilities for military personnel.

Additionally, military and civilian personnel will be working with tripod-mounted communications and radar equipment. All equipment will be used to assess interoperability and performance of various communications and radar system configurations. Military radio frequencies involved in the testing will not interfere with other frequencies or electronic communications in the area. During this event, mariners can expect many small, unmanned surface, sub-surface and air vehicles in operation. All these unmanned platforms will have manned vessels in the vicinity for control and safety. If members of the public see vessels in the water or unmanned airborne systems, please do not attempt to approach, touch or interfere with them.

WHO: Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering, Quantum and Battlefield Information Dominance; NSWC Crane; Michigan National Guard; NOAA; Army Development Command C5ISR Center; Air Force Test Center; and Naval Information Warfare Center Atlantic.

text:
Momentum is building on Capitol Hill to improve TRICARE’s coverage of autism care.

“Our military families, especially those with autistic children or children with other developmental disabilities, are entitled to receive the best possible care,” Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) wrote in a recent letter to Pentagon leaders, calling on them to provide comprehensive applied behavior analysis (ABA) services to TRICARE beneficiaries diagnosed with autism.

ABA is an evidence-based behavioral therapeutic approach that has become a standard of care for many autistic individuals.

[TAKE ACTION: Ask Your Lawmakers to Improve TRICARE Coverage of Autism Care]

“By refusing to provide ABA therapy as a basic medical benefit, TRICARE is failing our service members and forcing overwhelmed families to navigate a frustrating bureaucratic maze just to secure limited life-changing care,” Gillibrand said in a press release announcing the letter. “The Defense Health Agency must dismantle these restrictive barriers immediately and permanently authorize full ABA therapy as a basic TRICARE benefit and adopt all of the NASEM recommendations to ensure autistic children of service members receive the full care they need.”

The letter cites an independent analysis by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) which assessed TRICARE’s Autism Care Demonstration (ACD). The MOAA-supported report recommends authorizing ABA as a TRICARE basic benefit, among numerous other improvements to autism care.

Challenges with TRICARE’s coverage of ABA were also highlighted in a recent NBC News report on a military family’s fight to secure coverage for their young son’s autism care.

“Since 2021, military families have struggled to access critical care for their children with autism, and by removing ABA therapy as a basic medical benefit under TRICARE, DHA has put undue burdens on service families,” Schmitt said in the release. “Implementing the NASEM recommendations will help better serve our military families and ensure they have options for care for their children with autism.”

[RELATED: NDAA Draft Would Reverse Planned Cuts, Closures at 41 Military Hospitals and Clinics]

The FY 2027 National Defense Authorization Act may also address ACD concerns. The House Armed Services Committee’s version of the annual bill includes a provision with Pentagon report requirements detailing progress on implementing NASEM recommendations. Increased congressional oversight is key to ensuring TRICARE follows through on ACD reforms.

title: TRICARE Coverage for Drug & Alcohol Rehab in San Diego, CA
description:
There is no overall lifetime limit on TRICARE coverage for medically necessary addiction treatment.
TRICARE plans in San Diego generally cover evidence-based addiction therapies as part of behavioral health treatment.
TRICARE plans in San Diego, can cover multiple levels of addiction treatment.
While TRICARE covers many evidence-based addiction treatment services, some treatments and expenses may not be covered.
How to Use TRICARE for Coverage Using TRICARE for addiction treatment begins with confirming eligibility, understanding available benefits, and finding a TRICARE-authorized treatment provider.
text:
What is TRICARE?

TRICARE is a government-funded health insurance program for active duty service members, National Guard and Reserve members, military retirees, and their eligible family members and survivors. Administered by the U.S. Department of Defense, it provides health coverage for a wide range of medical services, including primary care, specialty care, mental health services, and substance use disorder treatment through authorized military and civilian providers.

TRICARE Eligibility Rules

TRICARE is available to active duty service members, National Guard and Reserve members, military retirees, Medal of Honor recipients, and their eligible spouses, children, and survivors. Eligibility depends on military service status and enrollment in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System (DEERS), with available plans varying by beneficiary category.

There is no overall lifetime limit on TRICARE coverage for medically necessary addiction treatment. However, coverage is subject to plan rules, medical necessity requirements, prior authorization for certain services, and treatment at authorized TRICARE providers. Depending on the type of care, beneficiaries may also be responsible for copayments, cost-shares, or deductibles.

What Addictions Does TRICARE Cover in San Diego?

TRICARE may cover treatment for a wide range of substance use disorders when services are medically necessary. Covered addictions can include alcohol, opioids including prescription painkillers, heroin, and fentanyl, cocaine, methamphetamine, prescription medications, benzodiazepines, marijuana, hallucinogens, inhalants, synthetic drugs, and polysubstance use disorders. TRICARE’s mental health benefits may also support treatment for certain behavioral addictions, such as gambling, internet and social media use, video gaming, compulsive shopping, and pornography addiction, when these behaviors occur alongside a diagnosed mental health condition or substance use disorder.

What Addiction Therapies Will TRICARE Cover?

TRICARE plans in San Diego generally cover evidence-based addiction therapies as part of behavioral health treatment. Some plans may also include complementary therapies when they are integrated into a licensed treatment program.

TRICARE insurance may be able to cover:

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): Helps identify and change thought patterns and behaviors that contribute to substance use.

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT): Focuses on emotional regulation, distress tolerance, and reducing impulsive behaviors related to addiction.

Motivational Interviewing (MI): Strengthens internal motivation and commitment to recovery.

Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR): Addresses unresolved trauma that can drive substance use.

Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT): Encourages accepting difficult emotions while committing to healthier, recovery-focused actions.

Contingency Management (CM): Uses positive reinforcement to reward sobriety and treatment participation.

Psychoeducation: Teaches individuals about addiction, triggers, and relapse prevention strategies.

Medication-Assisted Treatment: Combines therapy with medications like Suboxone, Methadone, or Vivitrol to reduce cravings and withdrawal symptoms.

Individual Therapy: One-on-one counseling tailored to personal triggers and recovery goals.

Group Therapy: Peer-based sessions that build support, accountability, and shared insight.

Family Therapy: Helps repair relationships and strengthen a supportive home environment.

12-Step Facilitation: Introduces recovery principles used in programs like Alcoholics Anonymous.

Yoga Therapy: Supports stress reduction and mind-body awareness.

Art Therapy: Provides a creative outlet to process emotions and experiences.

Sound Therapy or Meditation: Helps regulate mood and reduce cravings.

Does TRICARE Cover Dual Diagnosis Treatment?

Yes, TRICARE may cover dual diagnosis treatment. Dual diagnosis, also known as co-occurring disorders, refers to the presence of both a substance use disorder and a mental health condition. Because these conditions often influence one another, treating only one without addressing the other can increase the risk of relapse and make long-term recovery more difficult.

Dual diagnosis treatment integrates addiction care with mental health treatment through a personalized plan that may include medical detox, inpatient or outpatient rehabilitation, medication-assisted treatment (MAT), psychiatric evaluation, medication management, individual therapy, group therapy, family counseling, and relapse prevention planning.

Common co-occurring mental health disorders treated alongside addiction include depression, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), borderline personality disorder (BPD), schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, panic disorder, and other trauma-related or mood disorders.

What Types of Rehab Will TRICARE Cover?

TRICARE plans in San Diego, can cover multiple levels of addiction treatment. Coverage is based on the severity of substance use, withdrawal risk, and mental health needs, and may include both inpatient and outpatient rehab services as part of a structured recovery plan.

Medical Detox (3 to 10 days): Supervised withdrawal management that helps individuals safely stop using drugs or alcohol while managing withdrawal symptoms with medical support.

Inpatient or Residential Treatment (14 to 90+ days): A highly structured program where clients live at the facility and receive 24-hour care, therapy, and medical supervision focused on stabilization and recovery.

Partial Hospitalization Program (PHP) (2 to 6 weeks): Intensive daytime treatment, typically 5 to 6 days per week for several hours per day, with clients returning home or to sober housing at night.

Intensive Outpatient Program (IOP) (4 to 12 weeks or longer): Flexible treatment several days per week for a few hours per session, designed for individuals stepping down from higher levels of care or needing structured support while living at home.

Outpatient Treatment (3 months to ongoing): Lower-intensity care with weekly or biweekly therapy sessions focused on relapse prevention, mental health support, and long-term recovery maintenance.

What Won’t TRICARE Cover?

While TRICARE covers many evidence-based addiction treatment services, some treatments and expenses may not be covered. In general, TRICARE does not cover services that are not considered medically necessary, experimental or unproven treatments, or care provided by unauthorized providers when authorization is required. Coverage may also be denied for luxury amenities, private rooms requested for convenience, non-medical wellness services, missed appointment fees, transportation not related to a covered medical service, and other expenses that fall outside the terms of a member’s plan.

How Much Does Rehab Cost Without Insurance in San Diego?

Rehab without insurance varies widely based on level of care, length of stay, and facility type. Medical detox usually costs about $1,000 to $8,000 for a short stay of 3 to 10 days, depending on medical supervision and withdrawal severity. Inpatient or residential rehab is the most expensive, typically ranging from $5,000 to $30,000 for 30 days, with luxury or high-end programs reaching $50,000 to $100,000+. Partial hospitalization programs generally cost around $7,000 to $15,000 per month, while intensive outpatient programs usually range from $3,000 to $10,000 for a full course of care.

Standard outpatient rehab is more flexible and lower cost, usually around $100 to $250 per therapy session, or approximately $1,500 to $11,000 total over several months depending on frequency. Aftercare and support groups are often free or very low cost.

Rehab cost is influenced by level of care, length of stay, facility type, medical needs like detox or dual diagnosis treatment, therapy intensity, location, staff qualifications, and whether the program is in-network with insurance or paid out-of-pocket.

How Long Can I Stay in Treatment With TRICARE?

The length of addiction treatment covered by TRICARE depends on medical necessity, treatment progress, diagnosis, and the level of care required. While there is no single time limit, typical treatment timelines include medical detox lasting about 3 to 10 days, residential inpatient treatment lasting approximately 14 to 90 days, partial hospitalization programs (PHP) lasting about 2 to 8 weeks, and intensive outpatient programs (IOP) lasting around 8 to 12 weeks. Outpatient therapy and continuing care may continue longer when clinically appropriate.

How to Use TRICARE for Coverage

Using TRICARE for addiction treatment begins with confirming eligibility, understanding available benefits, and finding a TRICARE-authorized treatment provider. Beneficiaries can review their plan details, contact TRICARE directly, or speak with a treatment program that accepts TRICARE. Many addiction treatment programs can verify insurance benefits, explain available coverage options, and help guide individuals through the admissions process. This process is confidential and reaching out to a treatment provider for information or an insurance verification does not automatically affect military benefits, eligibility, or enrollment status.

When choosing a provider that accepts TRICARE, individuals should look for an authorized treatment center that offers evidence-based addiction care and services that match their needs, such as detox, residential treatment, outpatient programs, medication-assisted treatment, mental health services, or dual diagnosis care. A treatment program can often confirm whether TRICARE coverage is available, explain any costs or authorization requirements, and help coordinate the next steps for care.

Beneficiaries may also contact TRICARE resources directly to verify coverage and locate authorized providers. Before starting treatment, it is important to confirm that the provider is authorized, understand what services are covered, and ask about any required referrals, approvals, deductibles, or cost-sharing responsibilities.

General Information About TRICARE

TRICARE was established in 1993 as the U.S. Department of Defense’s health care program to provide medical coverage for active duty service members, military retirees, and their eligible families. It replaced the former Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Uniformed Services (CHAMPUS) and expanded access to care through a combination of military treatment facilities and civilian health care providers.

Over time, TRICARE has evolved to offer several health plan options designed to meet the needs of different military populations. Current TRICARE plans include TRICARE Prime, a managed care option similar to a health maintenance organization (HMO); TRICARE Select, a preferred provider option that allows beneficiaries to choose their own providers; TRICARE For Life, which provides supplemental coverage for eligible Medicare beneficiaries; TRICARE Reserve Select for qualified Selected Reserve members; TRICARE Retired Reserve for certain retired Reserve members; TRICARE Young Adult for eligible adult children who have aged out of regular dependent coverage; and the US Family Health Plan, a TRICARE Prime option available in select areas.

TRICARE continues to provide coverage for a wide range of medical services, including preventive care, specialty treatment, mental health services, and substance use disorder treatment through authorized providers.

text:
SAN ANTONIO, Texas - The atmosphere at the 2025 Military Health System (MHS) Conference was electric, charged with the shared purpose of thousands of medical professionals dedicated to a singular mission: the health, survival, and readiness of the nation’s warfighters and their families. Amidst the briefings on medical logistics, battlefield trauma care, and clinical innovations, a moment of profound recognition was reserved for the trailblazers of Defense Health Network (DHN) Central.

These were not just names on a screen; they were the architects of high-reliability care, the quiet professionals working long shifts in stateside clinics, and the leaders shaping the future of military medicine.

“I would like to extend my heartfelt congratulations to our DHN Central recipients of 2025 Military Health System Awards, which were presented at last week’s MHS Conference,” said DHN Central Director Maj. Gen. Robert K. Bogart. “These honors reflect the exceptional dedication, leadership, and innovation demonstrated by our military health professionals and facilities across our Network.”

The Vanguard of Nursing and Patient Care

At the heart of any military medical facility is its nursing staff - the critical link between medical strategy and patient recovery. The MHS recognized four distinct leaders from DHN Central who set the gold standard for nursing excellence this year.

At Brooke Army Medical Center (BAMC), a hub of severe trauma care and complex medical operations, two leaders stood out.U.S. Air Force Maj. Kayla M. Rondina earned the Midgrade Military Nursing Leadership Excellence Award for her tireless work in managing complex clinical workflows, whileLawanda M. Clarkwas honored with the Senior Civilian Nursing Leadership Excellence Award, proving that civilian partners are the bedrock of continuity and expertise in military hospitals.

“It is a distinct honor to be recognized as Nurse of the Year, and receiving this news truly brought me to tears,” said Lawanda Clark who serves as the Clinical Nurse Officer in Charge, Brooke Army Medical Center.

“This award is a proud milestone in my 30-year career in OB, reflecting a lifetime of dedication to the BAMC mission of putting patient care and safety first. While this is an individual honor, it also reflects the privilege I have in leading and collaborating daily with a phenomenal team of GS civilians, active-duty members, and contractors who bring excellence, compassion, and professionalism to our unit. I am immensely proud of the leadership I provide in driving our simulation training, skills fairs, and the hands-on mentorship of our novice Air Force nurses and technicians. By championing evidence-based practice and fostering seamless collaboration with our residents, we are successfully shaping the next generation of clinicians together. I want to thank my incredible supervisory team and the BAMC leadership team for this incredible honor, which stands as a deeply meaningful testament to my hard work, my leadership of a large and dedicated team, and my unwavering commitment to our mission.”

Across the network, senior military nursing leaders were also called to the stage.U.S. Army Lt. Col. Angela B. Samosorn, Bassett Army Community Hospital, andU.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Jennifer L. Varney, McConnell Military Medical Treatment Facility were both awarded the Senior Military Nursing Leadership Excellence Award. Their command presence and clinical mastery have ensured that their respective facilities remain ready to deploy care at a moment's notice.

Allied Health and the Enlisted Backbone

Military medicine is a massive, synchronized operation requiring diverse specialties and a robust enlisted corps. Recognizing the critical role of allied health professionals,U.S. Air Force Capt. Brendin B. Wood, Kirtland Military Medical Treatment Facility, was awarded the Junior Provider Allied Health Leadership Excellence Award, representing the innovative approaches young officers are bringing to specialized patient care.

Yet, as any commander knows, the enlisted corps is the backbone of the military. The MHS Enlisted Leadership Excellence Awards highlighted two outstanding Airmen who embodied the core values of service and excellence.U.S. Air Force Tech. Sgt. Crystal B. Whiterock, Wilford Hall Ambulatory Surgical Center, was named the Vanguard Non-commissioned Officer, a testament to her hands-on leadership and clinical sharpness.

Meanwhile,U.S. Air Force Senior Master Sgt. Andria C. McGuire, Luke Military Medical Treatment Facility, took home the Leadership Excellence Senior Non-commissioned Officer award, recognized for her strategic vision and mentorship of the next generation of medics.

“For me, operational readiness and patient care are not competing priorities, they are complementary responsibilities,” said McGuire, who serves as the Senior Enlisted Leader for the Luke Medical Dental Support Squadron.

“Every patient encounter is an opportunity to sharpen the clinical skills, critical thinking, and professionalism our Airmen will rely on in deployed environments. I focus on creating a culture where readiness is integrated into daily operations through deliberate training, realistic exercises, mentorship, and accountability. By investing in our people and ensuring they understand the direct connection between their daily duties and the mission, we maintain a medically ready force capable of providing exceptional care both at home station and anywhere the nation calls us to serve.”

“I am deeply honored to receive this recognition, but I view it as a reflection of the incredible teams I have had the privilege to serve alongside throughout my career,” McGuire said. “I believe my selection was influenced by a commitment to servant leadership, mission excellence, and developing others. Whether improving operational readiness, enhancing patient care, or building partnerships within our communities, my focus has always been on creating lasting impact and empowering people to succeed. This award represents the dedication, professionalism, and resilience of the Airmen, civilians, and teammates who inspire me every day.”

Institutional Excellence: Transforming the System

The conference also zoomed out from individual accolades to recognize the systemic triumphs of entire facilities. High Reliability in healthcare means zero harm, consistent outcomes, and a culture of continuous improvement.

Elmendorf Military Medical Treatment Facilitydemonstrated a relentless pursuit of these principles, earning the Excellence in High Reliability Award for Inpatient MTF Most Improved. Thousands of miles away, the team atDavid Grant Medical Centerwas awarded the Excellence in High Reliability Award for Leadership Commitment, showcasing how top-down dedication to safety protocols transforms patient outcomes.

The Mission Continues

As the conference concluded and the awardees returned to their respective bases—from the frozen flightlines of Elmendorf to the busy corridors of BAMC—their awards served as a reminder of a broader truth.

These honors reflect more than individual brilliance; they represent the foundation of DHN Central's success. Through their unwavering dedication, professionalism, and daily efforts, these outstanding individuals and teams are advancing the readiness of the force, ensuring that whenever and wherever the nation calls, military medicine is ready to answer.

text:
Team members with the Defense Health Agency’s Warfighter Readiness, Performance, and Brain Health team hosted an end-user touchpoint at the Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, Tactical Medicine Training Center, June 30, 2026.

The event brought together U.S. Navy corpsmen and medical officers from across the II Marine Expeditionary Force to assess new capabilities for evaluating traumatic brain injuries on the battlefield. Participants evaluated Traumatic Brain Injury Field Assessment Program devices in a hands-on session, giving TBI-FAP developers critical feedback directly from the frontline medical providers who may one day use the equipment in austere environments.

The TBI-FAP program is managed by brain health experts within the WRPBH Project Management Office in collaboration with partners at the North Carolina Center for Optimizing Military Performance. This event, the latest in a series, was designed to gather feedback on TBI assessment technology prototypes in development for use in a far-forward, operational environment. Feedback from prospective end users is a vital step in the early development of any program, according to Damien Hoffman, a product manager with WRPBH.

“Collaborating with stakeholders across the military services and from key organizations in a systematic, routine way is imperative to our team’s success,” said Hoffman. “These touchpoints allow us to gather an array of feedback from end users with varying degrees of experience and expertise, an invaluable resource as we develop products for the warfighter.”

During the assessment, Navy corpsmen and medical officers got hands-on with the candidate technologies to test usability, durability, and integration into existing tactical combat casualty care workflows.

"It is great, for me as a corpsman, to see what types of technologies are being developed for medical providers who operate at the front lines,” said Petty Officer 3rd Class Aspen Mitchell, a hospital corpsman with Marine Wing Communications Squadron 28 at Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, North Carolina. “Because of our expeditionary mission, we could literally be deployed anywhere in the world,and healthcare is vital for mission success. It is important for us, as medical providers, to give input on technologies during the development process to make the candidate technologies better and ensure they meet our needs as possible end-users.”

As the Department of War continues to prepare for possible Large-Scale Combat Operations in austere environments across the globe, ensuring warfighters have immediate access to neurological assessments is a top priority for military health leaders within the DHA. In future conflicts, medical providers anticipate a high likelihood of prolonged field care scenarios. Unlike operations over the last two decades where aeromedical evacuation was often rapid and guaranteed, near-peer conflicts in austere, remote locations will likely feature highly contested airspace and limited aviation resources.

For the Navy-Marine Corps team, these challenges are compounded by their unique role as the nation's premier amphibious force. Marines and their embedded Navy medical providers frequently operate in distributed, maritime environments—moving from ship to shore or securing expeditionary advanced bases across vast littoral regions. In these decentralized operational areas, the "golden hour" for traditional medical evacuation is often impossible to meet.

Because of these unique amphibious and logistical constraints, Navy corpsmen must be equipped to hold, monitor, and treat casualties at or near the point of injury for extended periods. The ability to accurately assess traumatic brain injuries on the front line using lightweight, organic tools – like those developed through the TBI-FAP – is critical. It empowers first responders to make vital triage decisions, manage complex neurological trauma while isolated on distant shores, and prioritize limited maritime MEDEVAC assets for the most critical cases.

“Our process is a continuum, with flexibility to evolve alongside emerging threats and meet the needs of frontline warfighters, combatant commands, and joint staff,” Hoffman said. “Our goal is to rapidly develop a TBI assessment capability at the speed of relevance, and these touchpoints are imperative to achieving that goal.”

title: TRICARE Dental Vs. TRICARE Medical Insurance Coverage - MyMilitaryBenefits
description:
TRICARE Dental Vs. TRICARE Medical Insurance Coverage Routine dental care is covered under the TRICARE Dental plan, but the surgeries required for some dental patients may be covered under the TRICARE medical plan instead.
But oral surgical procedures and treatments stemming from bodily injuries or medical diagnoses are managed under the primary TRICARE medical benefit, not TRICARE Dental.
Defining Routine Dental Care Under TRICARE Routine dental care includes preventive dental medicine, diagnostic, and common restorative treatments.
Routine dental care services are handled by dental insurance plans rather than standard TRICARE medical plans.
For routine dental care, the TRICARE Dental Program operates through a network and non-network provider system managed by United Concordia.
text:
Joe Wallace

The Defense Health Agency’s official site, DHL.mil, admits that using TRICARE can be confusing, especially in the gray area of coverage, such as what qualifies as routine dental care and what counts as surgery under TRICARE. How do you know if the procedure you need at the dentist’s office is covered and under which plan?

TRICARE Dental Vs. TRICARE Medical Insurance Coverage

Routine dental care is covered under the TRICARE Dental plan, but the surgeries required for some dental patients may be covered under the TRICARE medical plan instead.

TRICARE regulations determine which plan pays for services, what pre-authorization requirements apply, and how out-of-pocket expenses are calculated.

Routine and basic restorative services are managed through your dental insurance programs, such as the TRICARE Dental Program administered by United Concordia. But oral surgical procedures and treatments stemming from bodily injuries or medical diagnoses are managed under the primary TRICARE medical benefit, not TRICARE Dental.

Defining Routine Dental Care Under TRICARE

Routine dental care includes preventive dental medicine, diagnostic, and common restorative treatments. These are considered requirements for maintaining oral hygiene.

Routine dental care services are handled by dental insurance plans rather than standard TRICARE medical plans. Eligible family members, National Guard or Reserve personnel, and retirees enroll in these separate dental insurance options, each with its own premiums and annual benefit caps.

The TRICARE Dental Program covers up to two routine exams and cleanings within a one-year window. This benefit expands to three annual cleanings for pregnant beneficiaries. Other covered routine and restorative dental health services include:

Diagnostic tools, such as bitewing or full-mouth X-rays.

Standard fillings, crowns, and root canals to address localized decay or pulp infections.

Standard tooth extractions, including routine wisdom teeth removal.

Orthodontic treatments and braces are subject to specific age limits and lifetime cost limits.

These procedures require technical expertise, but do not qualify as medical treatments. They address problems confined to the teeth and their supporting structures.

>> Never miss a benefits update. Subscribe to the MyMilitaryBenefits Newsletter today.

Dental Care Vs. Dental Surgery

TRICARE medical plans cover oral procedures only when the care meets the definition of “adjunctive dental care,” which refers to limited, medically necessary dental treatment provided as part of the treatment of an otherwise covered medical condition, trauma, or disease. In these situations, the dentist or oral surgeon provides the care, but TRICARE treats the financial claim as a medical benefit.

Medical coverage applies when an oral issue results from external trauma or systemic disease, or when an oral procedure affects overall physical health:

If a patient suffers facial trauma resulting in a fractured jaw, a dentist may need to extract teeth to stabilize the bone structure. TRICARE medical plans cover the extraction, jaw surgery, and subsequent prosthodontic restoration of the missing teeth.

Surgery to treat, excise, or manage cancer inside the mouth or around the facial structures is billed to the medical benefit.

Corrective procedures for severe inherited conditions affecting the head and neck, such as cleft lip or palate, are covered by medical insurance. To qualify, the structural issue must cause functional impairment that hinders normal bodily processes.

Medical benefits apply to the surgical removal of tumors and cysts, treatment of infections that spread beyond the localized tooth socket, and surgeries involving the sinuses, salivary glands, or ducts.

Coverage Scenarios Under TRICARE

Coverage scenarios, according to the Defense Health Agency, include but may not be limited to the following, as displayed on DHA.mil:

Routine tooth cleaning or filling — Dental

Root canal due to infection — Dental

Braces for cosmetic reasons — Dental

Wisdom Teeth Removal — Dental

Tooth removal after facial trauma — Medical with pre-authorization

Surgery for a jaw fracture — Medical with pre-authorization

Removal of tooth fragments from soft tissue — Medical with pre-authorization

If a patient breaks or cracks a tooth during normal activities without suffering broader facial bone trauma, the medical benefit will not pay for the treatment. Repairing the cracked tooth in this scenario is a restorative dental responsibility under a dental insurance plan.

For temporomandibular joint (TMJ) syndrome, TRICARE medical plans provide limited coverage focused strictly on medical management and immediate pain relief. Covered medical services include initial diagnostic X-rays, the construction of an occlusal splint, physical therapy, and up to four initial office visits.

However, TRICARE medical plans strictly exclude permanent dental alterations for TMJ, including occlusal equilibration, orthodontics, or restorative occlusal rehabilitation.

Oral abscesses are handled as dental issues unless the infection spreads extensively beyond the immediate dental alveolus, at which point the deep infection elevates the situation to a medical status.

Pre-Authorization Requirements

Except in urgent medical emergencies, TRICARE medical plans require formal pre-authorization for so-called adjunctive dental care and oral surgeries. The treating provider must submit a request along with clinical documentation to the relevant regional TRICARE health plan contractor before the operation occurs. In an emergency, the pre-authorization mandate is waived for the essential care needed.

For routine dental care, the TRICARE Dental Program operates through a network and non-network provider system managed by United Concordia.

Using non-network providers often requires patients to pay the full fee upfront and file for reimbursement, which may leave them responsible for any charges that exceed the contract rates allowed. Before scheduling any dental or maxillofacial procedure, verify your TRICARE coverage options.

title: Military Health Care: Clinical Quality Management in Operational Settings Like Field Hospitals
description:
DOD health care providers deliver care where military operations and humanitarian missions take place.
DOD directed the Army, Navy, and Air Force to update their policies for managing health care quality in these settings.
The Navy has issued several policies on aspects of health care quality management.
Why GAO Did This Study DOD health care providers deliver critical health care services in settings where military operations take place.
To guide efforts to promote health, prevent harm, and provide high-quality care in the military health system, DHA issued a clinical quality management framework in 2019.
text:
DOD health care providers deliver care where military operations and humanitarian missions take place. Such "operational settings" include hospital ships, field hospitals, and aircraft carriers.

DOD directed the Army, Navy, and Air Force to update their policies for managing health care quality in these settings. The policies are supposed to help ensure that safety incidents are reviewed, potential provider misconduct is investigated, and more.

As of March 2026, the Army and Air Force had not issued updated policies. The Navy has issued several policies on aspects of health care quality management.

Exterior of a field hospital

An exterior view of the entrance to a U.S. Army field hospital.

What GAO Found

In 2023, the Department of Defense (DOD) directed the military departments—Army, Navy, and Air Force—to update their policies on clinical quality management to align with Defense Health Agency (DHA) procedures to ensure high-quality care in operational settings. In December 2024, GAO reported that the military departments had not yet issued policies, specifically on provider credentialing and privileging, and recommended that they do so. As of March 2026, GAO found that Army and Air Force had not issued updated policies, while Navy issued several policies on aspects of clinical quality management.

GAO maintains that the military departments’ updates to these policies will facilitate a more consistent approach to clinical quality in operational settings. These updates may require more time, as the military departments incorporate additional changes resulting from DOD’s October 2025 implementation of a universal provider privileging program (i.e., the process of reviewing a provider’s qualifications and granting permission to deliver specific services).

Examples of Operational Settings Include Navy Hospital Ships and Army Field Hospitals

For patient safety events and health care risk management investigations, Army and Air Force officials stated that their departments generally follow the processes outlined in DHA’s procedures manual as their policies are being updated. GAO also found that Navy’s policies—which have been updated—align with DHA’s procedures.

Patient safety events are incidents or conditions that could have resulted, or did result, in harm to a patient, such as a medication error or a wrong-site surgery. Events are entered into a patient safety reporting system and investigated accordingly.

Health care risk management activities primarily involve provider quality assurance investigations, which could originate from suspected provider misconduct, among other reasons. Army and Air Force leverage DHA for assistance for investigations; Navy relies on its medical staff for support.

Why GAO Did This Study

DOD health care providers deliver critical health care services in settings where military operations take place. These operational settings include hospital ships, field hospitals, and aircraft carriers. To guide efforts to promote health, prevent harm, and provide high-quality care in the military health system, DHA issued a clinical quality management framework in 2019. This framework consists of programs such as provider credentialing and privileging, patient safety, and risk management. Military departments are responsible for updating their policies to align with DHA’s framework and implementing these programs in operational settings.

A House Report accompanying the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 includes a provision for GAO to review how the military departments ensure clinical quality in operational settings. GAO reported in GAO-25-106445 on provider credentialing and privileging and recommended that the military departments issue updated policies, which they indicated would be included in overall clinical quality management policies for operational settings. In this report, GAO describes (1) the status of these military department policies on clinical quality management, (2) how the military departments report and manage patient safety events, and (3) how the military departments conduct health care risk management investigations.

GAO interviewed DHA and military department officials and reviewed relevant program documentation. GAO also reviewed available operational patient safety event data reported for fiscal years 2022 through 2024, the most recent available data at the time of this review. These data were not included due to DOD’s concerns about the sensitivity of these data.

For more information, contact Sharon M. Silas at silass@gao.gov.

Service members, veterans, and their families carry experiences most people never have to navigate. Asking for help with mental health or addiction on top of everything else takes real courage. If you’ve been putting off the first call because you weren’t sure what your benefits cover, we can answer those questions first.

How TRICARE Benefits Work for Rehab

TRICARE is the federal health care program serving active-duty service members, veterans, retirees, and their families. It covers behavioral health treatment, including substance use disorder and mental health care, under federal mental health parity rules. Most TRICARE plans include outpatient rehab as a covered benefit, though the specifics depend on which plan you have and whether prior authorization is required.

We’re among the rehab centers that accept TRICARE in Portland, which means your behavioral health benefits apply directly to care here. What you actually pay depends on your plan type, your deductible status, and your coinsurance rate. The fastest way to get a clear picture of your coverage is to let our team verify it for you at no cost and with no obligation.

What TRICARE Covers for Mental Health and Addiction in Portland

TRICARE-approved rehab at Shanti Recovery & Wellness covers a range of conditions that frequently show up together in people connected to military service. Mental health treatment for depression, anxiety, PTSD, and trauma is covered under most TRICARE plans, as is outpatient addiction treatment for substance use disorders. For many people in this community, those conditions don’t show up separately.

People connected to military service face some of the highest rates of PTSD, depression, and substance use of any population. Those conditions tend to reinforce each other in ways that make treating only one at a time less effective. TRICARE recognizes integrated behavioral health treatment as a covered benefit for exactly this reason. When mental health and substance use get addressed together, the outcomes tend to hold up better over time.

Treatment Programs Available Through TRICARE at Shanti Recovery & Wellness

Most people coming in through TRICARE have questions about what the programs actually look like day-to-day. Everything here is provided on an outpatient basis, with telehealth available to Oregon residents who need it. The first step is always a psychiatric evaluation, because what someone actually needs isn’t always what they expected going in. Sometimes it’s more straightforward than people feared. Sometimes there’s more going on beneath the surface. Either way, the evaluation shapes what comes next.

The following programs are commonly covered under TRICARE:

Drug Addiction Treatment: Outpatient psychiatric care for substance use disorder, including evaluation, medication management, and therapy for co-occurring conditions driving the use.

Alcohol Addiction Treatment: Comprehensive outpatient care for alcohol use disorder, with attention to the mental health conditions that frequently accompany it.

Mental Health Treatment: Psychiatric evaluation and treatment for depression, anxiety, PTSD, ADHD, and other conditions, including TMS therapy for treatment-resistant depression where appropriate.

Dual Diagnosis Treatment: Integrated care for co-occurring mental health and substance use disorders addressed together within one coordinated psychiatric plan.

Every plan here gets adjusted as things change rather than following a fixed schedule. Providers stay involved throughout rather than stepping back after the initial evaluation, and families are included where it makes clinical sense. For people connected to military service, what’s driving the presenting concerns often runs deeper than what shows up on the surface. Care here is built to reflect that reality.

Who Qualifies for TRICARE Benefits

TRICARE coverage for addiction treatment is available to a broader group than many people realize. You may qualify if you fall into one of the following categories:

Active-duty service members

Veterans

National Guard and Reserve members

Retired service members

Eligible spouses and dependent children

Military service shapes how people experience mental health and addiction in ways civilian treatment programs don’t always account for. Care here starts with understanding those connections, not just the presenting symptoms. Whether you’re active duty, a veteran, or a family member carrying some of the same weight, you don’t have to explain yourself before getting help.

How to Verify Your TRICARE Coverage

Most people who call to verify benefits are surprised by how straightforward the process actually is. Our team contacts TRICARE directly, confirms your coverage levels, deductible status, coinsurance amounts, and any prior authorization requirements, and walks you through what it all means for your situation. Verify your TRICARE coverage with us before your first appointment. Have your TRICARE member ID card ready when you call. Same-day answers are common.

FAQs About Our TRICARE Addiction Treatment

Does TRICARE cover telehealth addiction treatment in Portland?

Most TRICARE plans cover telehealth for outpatient behavioral health services, including addiction and mental health care. Coverage specifics vary by plan, so verifying your benefits confirms exactly what applies to remote appointments.

Will TRICARE cover treatment if I’ve used behavioral health benefits before?

Yes, prior use of benefits doesn’t disqualify you from coverage. Each plan year resets, and coverage is determined by current clinical need rather than treatment history.

Does TRICARE cover both addiction and mental health treatment at the same time?

How long does TRICARE prior authorization typically take?

Authorization timelines vary depending on the plan and level of care requested. Our admissions team handles the authorization process directly with TRICARE and keeps you updated so there are no unexpected delays.

title: I'm 67 with a $140000 pension. Should I wait until 70 to claim Social Security so my wife gets more?
description:
Dear Quentin, The news lately has been about the Social Security trust fund going broke in 2032.
I'm now 67 and trying to determine when I should take Social Security.
Retired at 67 Related: 'I claimed Social Security at 62': At 76, I'm working at Walmart.
You could also invest your Social Security benefits if you claim at 67.
Can I avoid paying taxes on my Social Security benefits?
text:
By Quentin Fottrell

'When I pass, all my retirement income is reduced to $30,000 a year'

"How do I balance the decision to draw sooner based on a potential cutback in future benefits?" (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Quentin,

The news lately has been about the Social Security trust fund going broke in 2032. I'm now 67 and trying to determine when I should take Social Security. My wife and I have worked hard, saved and invested as much as we could. We consider ourselves fortunate for the position we're in.

I have a military retirement benefit as well as a state retirement benefit. I'm also a disabled veteran and receive a disability payment. All told, my income is around $140,000 a year. My wife works, but it's more her personal preference and doesn't generate any significant income.

I have a Medicare Advantage plan and Tricare for life. My wife uses Tricare as well. Medical costs, therefore, are largely covered. We both have long-term-care insurance policies, so we are on solid ground when it comes to our late-in-life coverage.

Our stock and mutual-fund portfolios, which include both regular IRAs and Roth IRAs, are at $2.5 million, depending on the market. We have about $600,000 equity in a house as well. We owe around $50,000 on two automobiles.

My wife is 62 and already started collecting her Social Security. It's worth $1,500 a month. If I start drawing Social Security now, it would be worth $3,000 a month. If I wait until my full retirement age, it will be $3,420 a month. If I wait until 2030, when I am 70, it would be $4,338.

The conundrum is that, when I pass, all my retirement income will be reduced to $30,000 a year for my wife, assuming she outlives me. How do I balance the decision to draw Social Security sooner based on a potential cutback in future benefits versus leaving the biggest payment I can give my wife if I pass first?

Our current income lets us live comfortably without relying much on the portfolio. We make occasional withdrawals for trips. The parents and grandparents on her side of the family have tended to live longer than the parents and grandparents on my side of the family.

Retired at 67

Related: 'I claimed Social Security at 62': At 76, I'm working at Walmart. Why do I still owe payroll taxes?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Assuming you predecease your wife, your Social Security payments will be more useful to her if you delay claiming than if you were to take them now.

Dear Retired,

It's a win-win whatever you decide.

In the event that you die before your wife, your Social Security payments will be more useful to her if you delay claiming than if you were to take them now. Given that your pensions and disability payments will drop to around $30,000 a year after your death, it makes sense to maximize your Social Security benefits.

A couple of reminders about the rules of survivor benefits: Your wife will get 100% of your Social Security benefit at full retirement age (67, in your case) even if you wait until 70 to claim. But if you do wait another three years, you'll get 8% more for each of those years. It seems like a short time to wait.

The breakeven point for delaying until 70 will occur roughly eight months after you turn 76. By claiming benefits immediately, you would get over $23,000 over the next three years. If you wait until 70, your monthly benefit would increase to $4,338. If you die before reaching your breakeven age, claiming at 67 would give you a higher total benefit.

After your death, your wife can claim survivor benefits on what your Social Security payments would be at your full retirement age, so she will get the same amount whether you claim now or at 70. (In order to get spousal benefits during your lifetime - up to 50% of your benefits if that amount is higher than 100% of her benefits - she would have to wait until you claim.)

You already have enough money to live on. That $140,000 a year is a comfortable retirement. Plus, you have $2.5 million in IRAs and mutual funds. You don't say how much is in Roth versus traditional accounts, but it's a nice complement to your income. You could also invest your Social Security benefits if you claim at 67.

Double-check the terms of the survivor options of your military pension and state pension. Some pensions offer substantial survivor benefits if the retiree elected them at retirement, while others don't. If what you say is correct, you don't have a big reason to hold off on claiming your Social Security to make the most out of your survivor benefits.

Don't miss: 'I get $1,460 in Social Security': My millionaire ex-husband, 74, refuses to pay alimony. What can I do?

A cautionary note on healthcare

A few words of caution on your healthcare coverage. Combining a Tricare for Life military healthcare plan with Medicare Advantage adds extra benefits like dental, vision and even gym memberships, but Medicare Advantage is the primary payer, so you don't get original Medicare freed from the shackles of networks. With Medicare Advantage, you must stick with an approved list of doctors and medical centers.

For those who may not be familiar with Medicare: Original Medicare is the government-run, fee-for-service program (Parts A and B) accepted by most healthcare providers. Medicare Advantage (Part C) is offered by private insurers and bundles hospital, medical and prescription-drug coverage (Parts A, B and often D).

More than 35 million seniors - roughly half of all Medicare beneficiaries - are enrolled in Medicare Advantage. An increasing number of medical centers are turning away Medicare Advantage patients for certain treatments because the reimbursement rates are too low to cover the cost of care. There is also a complex authorization process.

Family history is important when it comes to longevity, but it's not a zero-sum game. There's a lot you can do to make the most of your chances to live a longer life, including getting regular checkups, quizzing your primary-care physician about your bloodwork and, for men, getting your prostate checked every few years.

Finally, talk to your wife and your financial adviser. Whatever you decide, given your finances, your choices of claiming Social Security now or taking it later are both on the table. Whatever happens, the result won't be horrible. Congress has intervened in the past to prevent Social Security from running out of funds.

And as much as we try, no one can predict the future.

Related: 'We're worried the honey pot will run dry': Does the government borrow from my Social Security to fund federal programs?

text:
The Planning and Environment Court approved TriCare’s amended redevelopment of the former Sullivan Nicolaides site on Seven Oaks Street in late 2019. However, the existing buildings remain fenced and vacant. Nearby residents continue to raise concerns about trespassing, damage, graffiti, and nighttime activity.

Read: Tricare’s Amended Taringa Development Plans Approved

Those concerns resurfaced in a recent discussion in the Taringa & St Lucia Community Facebook group in July 2026. The community asked why demolition and construction had not begun, despite the project receiving approval years ago.

The latest debate reflects a change in local concerns. Earlier discussion focused on the size and design of the proposal. Now, locals want to know when work will start and how the site will be managed until then.

The Long Road to Development Approval

TriCare lodged plans in 2017 to replace the former pathology facility with a retirement living and aged care development. The proposal attracted hundreds of public submissions and significant attention across Brisbane’s inner west. Public submissions and campaign material raised concerns about height, scale, traffic and neighbourhood character.

Protect Taringa organised meetings and argued that its campaign opposed the size of the proposal, rather than aged care development itself. Brisbane City Council refused the original application. TriCare then appealed the decision to the Planning and Environment Court.

In late 2019, the court approved an amended proposal.

Council’s Development.i register also lists later applications and compliance matters connected with the property. These records show that planning work continued after the court decision. However, they do not provide a confirmed construction date.

No major demolition or construction was visible in the recent photographs shared by residents.

Community Attention Turns to the Vacant Buildings

In the latest community discussion, commenters focused mainly on site security and neighbourhood safety. Several people reported ongoing trespassing, vandalism and graffiti at the vacant buildings. Others referred to broken glass, noise and repeated calls to Queensland Police over several years.

Commenters expressed concern about children, pedestrians and nearby households. Some said the property continued to attract trespassers despite the added security.

A recurring message in the discussion was the need for a lasting solution.

Calls Grow for a Long-Term Solution

Residents supported demolition as a long-term response. Others argued that the property owner should continue securing the site while plans for redevelopment move forward.

A resident said that further fencing and security patrols would not provide a permanent solution. He called for greater transparency about why demolition had not proceeded. The resident had asked TriCare, which had allegedly previously advised him that demolition could affect the stability of the site. He also said he had asked to see supporting engineering material but had not received it.

Publicly available materials reviewed does not clearly explain what is preventing demolition or construction.

Ongoing Advocacy as Concerns Continue

Brisbane City Councillor Penny Wolff responded to residents in the Facebook discussion. She said she had advocated to TriCare. She also said she wanted the buildings demolished as soon as possible.

Ms Wolff listed fencing, screening, lighting, cameras, regular clean-ups and security patrols among the measures introduced at the site. She encouraged residents to keep reporting incidents to Queensland Police so each event could be recorded. Ms Wolff also said she had been advised that no local laws or safety regulations were being breached.

Commenters acknowledged that measures had been introduced. However, several said they had not delivered a permanent solution.

Read: Progress in Addressing Community Concerns at TriCare Site in Taringa

Planning records list several applications and compliance matters lodged after the 2019 approval. Those filings show ongoing administrative activity, but they do not confirm when work will start, nor do they provide a demolition date or a construction timetable.

Ms Wolff has previously said TriCare advised her that it remained committed to the development.

title: OIG Report: VA's Aggressive Deployment of AI in the Clinical Field Considered 'Risky'

text:
WASHINGTON, DC — VA policy to minimize the barriers preventing employee use of artificial intelligence (AI ) might be resulting in higher risks for veterans, according to a recent VA Office of the Inspector General report. An investigation found that the agency failed to acknowledge the extent to which providers are using AI chat tools in patient care.

While the tools are considered minimally risky for veterans, their use in the clinical field qualifies them as “high-impact” the report argued. OIG considered the danger significant enough that it released an advisory to VA physicians in February based on its preliminary findings.

In hearings before Congress, VA leaders have described VA’s emerging policy to “aggressively deploy” AI technology within the department. This is in line with Office of Management and Budget guidance released in April 2025 that directed agencies to “remove unnecessary and bureaucratic requirements that inhibit innovation and responsible adoption.”

According to one VA AI leader interviewed by OIG for the report, this guidance has been interpreted as a directive to “push risk management down to the lowest reasonable level.”

The OMB memorandum requires agencies to identify high-impact use cases and “implement minimum risk management practices” for employee use of that technology. When it comes to VA, an AI project is considered high-impact when it serves “as a principal basis for decisions or actions with legal, material, binding or significant effect on human health and safety.”

For example, VA’s Ambient AI Scribe, which listens to clinical visits and drafts medication notes, is considered a high-impact tool. Currently in the pilot stage, project safeguards include: conducting predeployment testing; completing AI impact assessment, conducting ongoing monitoring for performance and potential adverse impacts; ensuring adequate training; providing additional human oversight; offering consistent remedies and appeals; and incorporating feedback from end users and the public.

VA GPT and Microsoft Copilot Chat—both broadly available to VA staff—have not been classified high-impact. However, OIG’s investigation found that both are being used in clinical-care situations. Of 135 prompts shared on an AI-focused VA Teams site, 79 were identified as clinical in nature (56 for clinical notes, 17 for summarization and 6 for another purpose).

Studies of generative AI use in the medical field have found that poor prompt technique can result in output errors such as hallucinations—when an AI system presents false information as factually accurate. This can lead to incorrect information being placed in the patient record that impacts patient diagnosis and management.

The investigation also found that the Joint Patient Safety Reporting system used to capture medical errors, close calls and near misses did not have an AI-specific labelling process.

“Without a way to tag or trace AI-generated documentation, VA cannot readily detect patterns, investigate AI-generated safety events or implement quality improvement processes that may lead to safer prompting,” the report stated.

VA has responded to OIG’s findings by working with the Defense Health Agency to enable tagging of AI-related events. It’s also taken steps to increase communication between its AI-focused programs and the National Center for Patient Safety (NCPS).

According to VA, NCPS acknowledges the need to recognize when AI is a contributing factor during root causes analysis and will develop an education campaign to encourage recognition and reporting of AI-related patient safety events.

As for adverse events that have already occurred, a search by OIG investigators of the Joint Patient Safety Reporting system found no mentions of AI, and according to the report VA does not have a means of identifying records created with AI to retroactively identify potential patient safety concerns.

“It’s very tricky,” one NCPS AI lead told investigators. “We don’t have the best answer yet.”

According to VA, as of January 2026, the agency had 367 AI use cases in its inventory, with 253 existing within VHA. Of those, 68% were considered high-impact.

text:
A Call for Decisive Transformation in Military Medical Readiness

Last month, more than 2,600 military health professionals gathered in Dallas for the annual Military Health System Worldwide Conference. "Our mission is readiness," declared Assistant Secretary of Defense for Health Affairs Keith Bass. "We have a no-fail mission." He also warned against the "Walker Dip" named for Admiral Alasdair Walker, former British Surgeon General, who aptly observed that throughout history, military medical teams repeatedly fail to maintain "steady state readiness." The diagnosis is exactly right, and the prescription was laid out before the Senate Armed Services Committee in March 2025. Now we must find the institutional will to act.

We can also look to history to frame the type of commitment required to achieve decisive transformation. When Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico in 1519, legend holds that he gave the order to “burn the ships,” eliminating the option of retreat with a statement of absolute commitment. The enduring lesson: in the face of extreme challenges, victory requires a willingness to persevere with no easy outs.

The current structure of the Military Health System (MHS) has struggled to optimize both routine beneficiary care and wartime trauma readiness simultaneously. To retain our strategic edge in this no-fail mission, combat medical readiness cannot remain a secondary byproduct of routine, low-acuity healthcare delivery. It's time to implement durable fixes that guarantee outstanding care for troops in combat on day one of future wars. It's time to burn the ships.

The next major conflict will barely resemble past experience. Future large-scale combat operations against peer adversaries will produce casualty volumes and injury complexity on the scale of World War II — approximately 1,000 casualties per day for 100 consecutive days or longer. Evacuation timelines will stretch well beyond the golden hour in a contested battlespace. Blood product collection and storage will prove nearly impossible. Surgical teams will move underground to avoid becoming targets.

Yet our current MHS is not designed to meet these harsh demands. Most military treatment facilities (MTFs) do not manage sufficient trauma volume to sustain wartime proficiency. Today, fewer than 10% of military general surgeons meet even a minimal clinical readiness threshold, and the MHS cannot bridge this gap through low-volume practice or episodic training rotations. Expertise in modern combat casualty care demands full immersion, not intermittent exposure.

This readiness gap has created a demoralized workforce and significant talent attrition. A 2024 RAND Corporation study found that physicians leave after their service obligations primarily because of pay disparity, administrative burden, and clinical skill degradation. The Department of Defense's Inspector General verified this systemic failure, reporting that the military services routinely assign critical wartime specialists to low-volume locations without any regard for their clinical readiness requirements. Thus, it’s hardly surprising that the first question military physicians often ask each other is not “What drives you to serve” but rather "When do you get out?"

To enable decisive transformation, we present a three-part solution.

First, aggressively embed active-duty critical wartime specialties into America’s busiest civilian trauma systems. Military partnerships with high-volume civilian trauma centers must become the gold standard of deployment readiness. Military clinicians should belong to these centers operationally, contributing daily to high-acuity patient care while maintaining their deployable identity and command integration.

Second, optimize the domestic MTF footprint. Most MTFs should be refocused toward what they do best — beneficiary care, pre- and post-deployment health, rehabilitation, and force health maintenance. Simultaneously, a select number of strategically designated flagship MTFs should be fully resourced as national trauma readiness hubs. A recent GAO report noted the MHS maintains only Level I trauma center among the 725 MHS facilities, Brooke Army Medical Center. Additional sites — like Madigan and Walter Reed — must grow into their full potential by managing civilian trauma in high volumes.

Third, rebuild the reserve workforce through a modern Volunteer Medical Service Corps. Looking to history once again, when the United States entered World War I, the active Army had just 491 doctors. To scale the force, military and political leaders partnered with the American College of Surgeons and the American Medical Association to mobilize more than 30,000 physicians into uniform. Today, Congress must act with similar resolve to establish a modernized framework that allows regular reserve and individual mobilization augmentees to sustain wartime proficiency through daily practice at high-volume civilian trauma centers, backed by defined mobilization obligations and viable financial incentives. This will cost money; not acting now will cost lives.

Critics will note that military families depend on MTFs for healthcare, and they are right. Nothing in this proposal ends that access. Rather, it is a rejection of a status quo that is failing military medicine's core moral obligation: to safeguard the lives of our service members and bring America's sons and daughters home alive. To maintain our military medical edge in the current threat environment, Congress must mandate that the Pentagon embed its deployable teams where the trauma volume exists, expand its flagship military hubs to meet the mission, and bolster the reserve workforce.

It's time to burn the ships.

John M. Ruggero, DO is a trauma surgeon at Cook County Hospital in Chicago, IL where he serves as the Section Chief of Joint Combat Education and Training and surgeon champion for the U.S. Navy/Cook County Health Military Civilian Partnership. He served a combat tour during Operation Inherent Resolve and separated from active duty in the U.S. Navy in 2025 after 16 years of service.
